difficultyReason: One-move argument: a student cited every source and therefore did not plagiarize. The principle that cites-every-source entails no-plagiarism maps directly onto the conclusion.
stimulus: Professor: Mei's term paper included quotations and paraphrases from several books, but she provided a complete citation for every such passage. So Mei did not plagiarize in writing this paper.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the professor's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A writer who cites every source from which she borrows has not plagiarized.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Students should be required to include a bibliography with every term paper.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A paper that relies heavily on paraphrase demonstrates less original thought than one that does not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Plagiarism should be punished more severely than other forms of academic dishonesty.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A writer who fails to cite any source has committed plagiarism.

explanations.correct: The premise is that Mei cited every borrowed passage; the conclusion is that she did not plagiarize. Principle A bridges exactly that gap — citing every source means no plagiarism.
explanations.B: Off-topic — bibliographies are not the professor's subject.
explanations.C: Reversed — this would weaken an endorsement of the paper, not justify the no-plagiarism verdict.
explanations.D: Tangential — severity of punishment is irrelevant to whether plagiarism occurred.
explanations.E: Converse error — says what counts as plagiarism, not what rules it out; doesn't license the conclusion that Mei did not plagiarize.

difficultyReason: One-move ethical argument: a doctor who warned a patient of every material risk acted ethically. Principle maps patient-informed-of-risks to ethical conduct.
stimulus: Ethicist: Before the surgery, Dr. Okafor explained to her patient every material risk the operation carried. She therefore acted ethically in proceeding with the procedure.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A physician acts ethically in proceeding with a surgery only if the patient survives the procedure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A physician who informs a patient of every material risk before a procedure acts ethically in performing it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A physician who fails to disclose at least one material risk has acted unethically.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A physician should always recommend the least invasive procedure available.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients should be encouraged to seek second opinions before major surgery.

explanations.correct: The premise is full disclosure of material risks; the conclusion is that the doctor acted ethically. Principle B licenses that move directly.
explanations.A: Too narrow and off-topic — survival is not the ethicist's criterion.
explanations.C: Converse — it tells us when a doctor acts unethically, not what suffices for ethical conduct.
explanations.D: Tangential — the argument is not about procedure selection.
explanations.E: Off-topic — second opinions are not the ethicist's concern.

difficultyReason: One-move economic argument: the city should fund a library branch because more residents would use it than any other proposed project. Principle connects maximal use to funding priority.
stimulus: Columnist: Of all the public projects the city is considering, the proposed east-side library branch would be used by more residents than any other. The city council should therefore fund the library branch before funding any of the other projects.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the columnist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A public project should be funded only if it generates revenue for the city.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A public project should be funded before other proposed projects when it would be used by more residents than any of them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Public libraries provide greater long-term benefit to a community than most other public projects do.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any public project that is used by a majority of residents is worth funding.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Public funding priorities should be set by referendum rather than by the city council.

explanations.correct: The premise is comparative use; the conclusion is funding priority. Principle B directly ties highest-use to funding-first.
explanations.A: Tangential — revenue is not the columnist's criterion.
explanations.C: Too narrow and source-specific — rests on a claim about libraries that the columnist didn't make.
explanations.D: Mismatch — the columnist compares projects, not thresholds; 'most-used' does not imply 'majority uses it'.
explanations.E: Reversed — this would undermine the columnist's instruction to the council.

difficultyReason: One-move environmental argument: a regulation that reduces pollution without raising consumer costs should be adopted. Principle maps both features directly to the adoption conclusion.
stimulus: Environmental analyst: The proposed tailpipe rule would measurably reduce urban air pollution, and independent studies show that it would not raise consumer vehicle prices. The agency should therefore adopt the rule.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the environmental analyst's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A regulation should be adopted whenever it is favored by a majority of affected consumers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any regulation that fails to reduce pollution should be rejected.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A regulation that would reduce pollution and would not increase consumer prices should be adopted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Regulatory agencies should consider consumer prices only after assessing environmental impact.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No regulation should be adopted unless it eliminates the pollution it targets entirely.

explanations.correct: The analyst cites two features — pollution reduction and no price increase — and concludes the rule should be adopted. Principle C fuses exactly those features into a sufficient condition for adoption.
explanations.A: Off-topic — consumer opinion is not a premise of the argument.
explanations.B: Reversed focus — tells us when to reject, not when to adopt.
explanations.D: Procedural principle about order of consideration — doesn't license the adoption conclusion.
explanations.E: Too strong — would block the proposed rule, which only reduces but does not eliminate pollution.

difficultyReason: One-move legal argument: evidence obtained without a warrant must be excluded. Principle maps warrantless-search to exclusion.
stimulus: Attorney: The laptop prosecutors intend to introduce against my client was seized by police officers who did not first obtain a search warrant. Therefore, the court must exclude the laptop from evidence at trial.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the attorney's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any evidence seized by police without a warrant must be excluded from trial.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Courts should exclude from trial any evidence whose authenticity cannot be verified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Police officers who conduct unlawful searches should face professional discipline.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Evidence obtained with a warrant is always admissible at trial.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A defendant is entitled to inspect every piece of evidence the prosecution intends to use.

explanations.correct: The premise is a warrantless seizure; the conclusion is mandatory exclusion. Principle A bridges that move exactly.
explanations.B: Off-topic — authenticity isn't the attorney's objection.
explanations.C: Tangential — officer discipline doesn't govern evidentiary admission.
explanations.D: Converse — tells us about evidence with warrants, not without.
explanations.E: Off-topic — inspection rights don't justify exclusion.

difficultyReason: One-move technology argument: a software update that fixes a known security flaw without introducing new bugs should be released. Principle maps both features to release.
stimulus: Lead developer: Version 4.2 of our messaging app patches a known security vulnerability, and internal testing has found that it introduces no new bugs. We should therefore release version 4.2 to all users.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the lead developer's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A software update should be released to users if it patches a known security vulnerability and introduces no new bugs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A software update should never be released until every known vulnerability has been patched.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Users are entitled to be notified of any security vulnerability that affects their software.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any software update that introduces a new bug should be withdrawn.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A development team should prioritize feature improvements over security patches.

explanations.correct: The developer cites two properties — patches a known vulnerability, no new bugs — and concludes the update should be released. Principle A combines exactly those properties into a sufficient condition for release.
explanations.B: Too strong — would block release because other unknown vulnerabilities may remain.
explanations.C: Tangential — user notification is not the argument's conclusion.
explanations.D: Reversed focus — tells us when to withdraw, not when to release.
explanations.E: Off-topic and contrary in spirit to the developer's reasoning.

difficultyReason: One-move history argument: a source that is contemporaneous and corroborated by independent records should be treated as reliable. Principle maps both features to reliability.
stimulus: Historian: The diary kept by Commander Alcantara was written during the campaign itself, and its account of the battle is confirmed by independent military records. Historians should therefore treat the diary as a reliable source about the campaign.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the historian's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A historical source written long after the events it describes should be treated as unreliable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Historians should rely only on sources written by participants in the events described.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A historical source written during the events it describes and corroborated by independent records should be treated as reliable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Military records are generally more reliable than personal diaries.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Independent corroboration is required for any claim about ancient history.

explanations.correct: The historian cites two properties — contemporaneous and independently corroborated — and concludes the diary is reliable. Principle C fuses exactly those into a sufficient condition for reliability.
explanations.A: Converse focus — tells us when to treat a source as unreliable.
explanations.B: Too narrow — would make corroboration irrelevant and doesn't reach reliability.
explanations.D: Ranking principle unrelated to the historian's argument; also could undermine treating the diary as reliable on its own.
explanations.E: Too narrow — limits its force to ancient history, while the campaign isn't said to be ancient.

difficultyReason: One-move linguistics argument: a borrowed word that has become widely used in a language should be listed in that language's dictionary. Principle maps wide use to inclusion.
stimulus: Lexicographer: Although the word 'savante' was originally borrowed from French, it is now used routinely by speakers of English in a wide range of contexts. English dictionaries should therefore list 'savante' as an English word.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the lexicographer's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A word borrowed from another language should be listed in a dictionary once it is used routinely in a wide range of contexts by speakers of the borrowing language.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A dictionary of a language should list only words native to that language.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dictionaries of any language should include words used by professional writers in that language.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A language's dictionary should omit words whose spelling has not been standardized.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Words that appear in formal publications belong in that language's dictionary.

explanations.correct: The lexicographer cites that a borrowed word is now used routinely across contexts by English speakers, and concludes English dictionaries should list it. Principle A maps those premises to the conclusion.
explanations.B: Reversed — would block inclusion of any borrowing, undermining the conclusion.
explanations.C: Too narrow — premises don't say professional writers use the word.
explanations.D: Off-topic — spelling standardization is not mentioned.
explanations.E: Mismatch — the premise is routine use by speakers generally, not appearance in formal publications.

difficultyReason: One-move arts argument: a museum that acquired a painting knowing it was stolen is obliged to return it. Principle maps knowing acquisition of stolen art to the return obligation.
stimulus: Art critic: The Vellmar Museum purchased the landscape by Odile even though its curators knew at the time of purchase that the painting had been stolen from its previous owner. The museum is therefore obliged to return the landscape to that previous owner.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the art critic's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A museum should refuse to display any work whose provenance is disputed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A museum that acquires a work it knows to have been stolen is obliged to return the work to the party from whom it was stolen.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Museums should compensate the original owners of any works they display.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Curators who knowingly purchase stolen works should be dismissed from their positions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A museum is obliged to return any work in its collection upon the previous owner's request.

explanations.correct: The premise is a museum's knowing acquisition of a stolen work; the conclusion is an obligation to return it. Principle B licenses that exact move.
explanations.A: Off-topic — concerns display, not return of ownership.
explanations.C: Too broad — would require compensation even for legitimately acquired works.
explanations.D: Tangential — curator discipline doesn't settle the museum's obligation.
explanations.E: Too broad — would require return regardless of knowledge or theft.

difficultyReason: One-move policy argument: a tax credit that achieves its stated goal at lower cost than any alternative should be renewed. Principle maps both features to renewal.
stimulus: Policy advisor: The rural-broadband tax credit met its goal of extending high-speed internet to underserved towns, and it did so at a lower cost to the treasury than any alternative program would have. The legislature should therefore renew the credit.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the policy advisor's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A tax credit that has met its stated goal at a lower cost than any alternative program would have should be renewed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A tax credit should be renewed only if a majority of voters favor its renewal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any program that has failed to meet its stated goal should be allowed to expire.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tax credits are generally preferable to direct government spending.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A program should be renewed whenever the constituents it serves request renewal.

explanations.correct: The advisor cites that the credit met its goal and did so at the lowest cost, and concludes the legislature should renew it. Principle A maps those two features directly to the renewal conclusion.
explanations.B: Off-topic — voter approval is not a premise.
explanations.C: Converse focus — tells us when to let programs expire, not when to renew.
explanations.D: Too broad — a general preference for tax credits doesn't license renewing this particular one.
explanations.E: Off-topic — constituent requests aren't mentioned in the argument.
